title: Rematch Season: The Fights You Thought Were Behind You
subtitle: Dawn runs, worn tape, and a final girl who gets a call she should have let go to voicemail
excerpt: This week's watching runs from Homer to a slasher throwback, but the thread holding it together is the same one holding my hands together in wraps: nobody who's already been through it wants to go back in, and somebody always finds a reason to ask anyway.
intro_md:
Six-fifteen this morning, still dark, and I'm doing the loop past the canal that I've done so many times my legs have basically memorised it without asking my brain. Twenty minutes in, cold enough that my breath is doing more work than my calves, and I'm thinking about how every run like this is just a rematch with yesterday's run. Same route, same potholes, same spot by the lock where my pace always dips because I'm tired of pretending I'm not tired. Then it's straight to the gym for bag work, and by round four my hands are asking questions my head doesn't want to answer honestly.

That's the frame this week's films kept snapping into, whether they meant to or not. A hero who can't stop smiling through something that's clearly breaking him. A director sending her characters on a very long walk home. A family running the same desperate play on repeat because the alternative is worse. And one very good, very strange slasher that's really about what happens when somebody tracks down the woman who survived the worst night of her life and asks her to do it again, on camera, for money. I know that phone call. It's the one every journeyman gets eventually, usually from a promoter, usually with a number attached, usually right when the scar tissue had finally stopped talking to you.

film_blurbs.title: The Odyssey (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
I went into this expecting spectacle and came out thinking about roadwork, which tells you something about where my head's at these days. It's a long, physical film about a man who cannot simply stop moving, whose entire identity has become the distance between him and home, and who keeps taking hits that would sideline most people and just... continuing.

That's every marathon I've half-trained for and every twelve-round fight I've watched from ringside where a guy's legs go in round eight and he keeps them anyway because stopping is somehow scarier than finishing wrong. Homer's been quietly narrating distance running longer than distance running has existed as a hobby, and this adaptation gets that better than I expected. Going the distance isn't a finish line thing. It's a decision you keep making every single mile.

film_blurbs.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
Nobody warned me this one would land like a gut shot. There's a real sadness sitting underneath all the wall-crawling, the kind you only notice because you've felt it yourself walking out of a sparring session smiling at your corner while something inside you is quietly cataloguing every rib that just got tested.

The mask does a lot of work in this franchise, obviously, but here it felt less like a disguise and more like a mouthguard: something you bite down on so the people who love you don't see exactly how much you're taking. I know a few boxers who fight with that exact same face on. Cheerful right up until the bell, then very, very quiet on the walk home.

film_blurbs.title: The End of Oak Street (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
David Robert Mitchell trades dread-drenched suburbs for something colder and more survivalist here, and there's a stretch in the middle where a character just keeps trying the same failing plan, over and over, with the same tools, expecting a different result. I won't pretend I didn't laugh a little, in the specific way you laugh at something that's basically autobiography.

That is genuinely most of my jab work. Same shoulder, same snap, same target, round after round, and my coach standing there saying 'again' like it's a complete sentence. It usually is. The film is more patient than I am about letting that repetition pay off, but I respected it for trusting the grind to eventually mean something, even when everything on screen is telling you it might not.

film_blurbs.title: Tony (2026)
film_blurbs.body_md:
This one snuck up on me. It's ostensibly about somebody else entirely, but the film keeps getting stolen out from under itself by a supporting performance as a line cook working double shifts in a bandana, sweating through service like it's the tenth round of a fight nobody's paying him enough to be in.

I have a soft spot for characters like that because I spend a lot of my life around the boxing equivalent: cutmen, corner assistants, the guy who wraps your hands at 6am and says nothing but somehow tells you everything about how the day's going to go. Nobody writes their name on the poster. The film knows exactly what it's got in him and gets out of his way, which is more generous than most scripts manage.

horror_deepdive.title: One More Round With the Final Girl
horror_deepdive.body_md:
Jane Schoenbrun's newest is dressed up as a slasher throwback, and it delivers on that promise, but the engine underneath it is something I recognise from twelve years of gym mornings: somebody comes back for the person who already survived once and asks them to do it again.

The setup hands a young director the keys to a dead franchise, ["a zombie IP," the "Little Death" franchise, a riff on Jason Voorhees, complete with a fictional camp called Miasma and a masked villain](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/teenage-sex-and-death-at-camp-miasma-jane-schoenbrun-film-review-2026). That's a reboot, sure, but it's also just the plot of every ageing fighter's comeback story with the serial numbers filed off. Somebody owns the rights to your name, your record, your one great night, and eventually somebody decides there's money left in booking it again.

The film makes the metaphor almost embarrassingly literal. [Kris journeys to the movie's iced-over summer camp to track down its original final girl, Billy (Gillian Anderson), and convince her to star in the remake](https://www.culturedmag.com/article/2026/08/12/film-camp-miasma-jane-schoenbrun-review/). Billy did not ask for this. Billy survived the worst night of her life and, by every reasonable measure, closed that door for good. Somebody found the door anyway and knocked, with a contract instead of a bouquet.

I've been in rooms with fighters getting that exact knock. A late-thirties journeyman who hasn't sparred properly in two years, still walking with a hitch from the last one, getting a call because a promoter needs a name on a undercard and the numbers work better if the name has history. The body remembers everything even when the calendar insists it's fine. Scar tissue doesn't forget who broke it. And the promoter on the other end of the phone is never lying to you exactly, they're just not the one who has to go the distance.

What makes the film sharper than a straightforward comeback story is how it refuses to keep the final girl role sitting still. [Through the film's surreal twists and turns, Kris herself effectively becomes a kind of final girl, even if it's not quite as simple as that](https://www.joblo.com/teenage-sex-and-death-at-camp-miasma-cannes-review/). That's the part that got me. It's not just that the veteran gets pulled back in. It's that the fresh talent chasing the veteran's legacy ends up standing in exactly the same ring, discovering the hard way that the title doesn't retire when the person holding it steps away. Somebody always inherits the fight.

Every gym has a version of Billy. The old head who does pads twice a week now, who will absolutely tell you the story of the one that made his name if you buy the coffee, who says no every single time somebody floats a comeback and then, occasionally, doesn't. Going the distance was never really about the twelfth round. It's about what you do with your life in the years after the bell, when the crowd's gone and somebody's still convinced there's one more good night left in you. Camp Miasma just puts a mask and a body count on a decision every journeyman eventually has to make for real.

closing_md: Hands are sore, legs are sorer, and I've got a session tomorrow where my coach is going to make me throw the same jab another three hundred times until it finally listens. See you next Friday.
